The doctor noted the review of systems sheet endorsed fatigue and a little dizziness. Positive symptoms discussed include fatigue, intermittent lightheadedness/dizziness, intermittent bloating, exertional shortness of breath, slight chest cramps, and slight cough. Ms. Cooper is a 65-year-old female and a new patient referred by Diane Nelson for long-standing iron deficiency anemia. She reports that around December she tried to donate blood and was told she was anemic; this was not the first time she had been told she was anemic. She reports being anemic since age 13. She also reports that her anxiety and depression have been worsening. The patient thinks this could be a thyroid problem. She had heavy periods until a hysterectomy in 1996. She reports her doctors have not told her why they think she is anemic. Last colonoscopy was about 5–6 years ago and was normal with no polyps; she was told to return in 10 years. She denies pacemaker/defibrillator, sleep apnea, and oxygen use at night. Alcohol use is once or twice a year. She started taking iron pills that she had not taken for about a year: ferrous sulfate 25 mg tablets twice daily, one in the morning and one in the evening. She also takes over-the-counter vitamin B12. She reports no prior issues with sedation, only sleepiness afterward.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: fatigue, feverish with chills at times, chilling sensations, cold intolerance.
Respiratory: exertional dyspnea and wheezing with activity.
Neurologic: headaches.
Psychiatric: worsening anxiety and depression.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General physical exam performed. Heart and lungs were auscultated. Abdomen was examined; no tenderness with palpation. Physical exam was normal without significant findings.

RESULTS
Follow-up blood work on 01/20/20 showed low hemoglobin, stable hematocrit, and normal iron labs, although ferritin was low. Prior colonoscopy about 5–6 years ago was normal with no polyps; she was told follow-up in 10 years.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Long-standing iron deficiency anemia, diagnosed in 12-2019 per the doctor’s dictation, with fatigue, chills, exertional dyspnea/wheezing, headaches, cold intolerance, and worsening anxiety/depression. The doctor suspects possible internal bleeding as a source of the anemia. The patient expressed concern that it could be a thyroid problem.

- If these tests are normal/inconclusive, consider capsule endoscopy (pill camera).
- Send referral to Dr. Flores, hematologist, to determine whether IV iron or something to help the body store iron better is needed; patient to schedule that appointment.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient reports sharp pain on the right side of the abdomen below the ribs for the last several days. The pain moves to the lower abdomen and into the groin. It comes and goes; when it comes, it is pretty bad and the patient feels like he cannot find a comfortable position. The patient reports burning with urination. He does not think there is any frank blood, but the urine sometimes looks a little dark. He has taken Tylenol, which has not really helped. He feels nauseated but is not vomiting. The patient’s father had kidney stones. The patient has had kidney stones before and has been able to pass them, but this episode is taking a lot longer. History includes a CT scan ordered by the primary care doctor that reportedly showed a kidney stone, with referral to urology. The doctor wondered if it might be gallstones.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Nausea, no vomiting. Fever and chills were not discussed.
Genitourinary: Burning with urination; urine sometimes dark; patient does not think there is frank blood.
Gastrointestinal: Right-sided abdominal pain below the ribs, moving to the lower abdomen and groin; nausea without vomiting.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Abdominal examination: no tenderness to palpation, no evidence of rebound or guarding, no peritoneal signs. Positive CVA tenderness on the right flank. The doctor explained that this means tenderness over the right kidney and that the patient might have some inflammation there.

RESULTS
The doctor reviewed the CT scan of the abdomen ordered by the primary care doctor. It shows a 0.5 centimeter kidney stone located in the proximal right ureter. There is no evidence of hydronephrosis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Acute nephrolithiasis (kidney stone), with a 0.5 centimeter stone in the proximal right ureter. The doctor initially wondered if the pain might be gallstones. Right flank CVA tenderness may suggest some inflammation, per the doctor.

Plan:
- Push fluids to help facilitate urination and help pass the stone.
- Prescribe oxycodone 5 milligrams every 6 to 8 hours as needed for pain; may continue to alternate with Tylenol.
- Provide a strainer to strain urine so the stone can be seen if it passes and sent for tests.
- Order basic metabolic panel, urinalysis, and urine culture.
- Follow up in 1 to 2 weeks. If still having symptoms, discuss further treatment such as lithotripsy, a shock wave procedure with sedation to break up the stone, or ureteroscopy, a small telescope/camera used to go up through the urethra and bladder into the ureter to retrieve the stone.
- Contact the doctor if symptoms worsen.
